triage.name: Overactive Bladder
triage.reason: Common syndrome of urgency, frequency and nocturia diagnosed clinically by history and voiding diary, with a broad differential to exclude.

demographics: More common in women than men
Prevalence increases with age in both sexes
More common in men with benign prostatic enlargement
comorbidities: Neurologic disease (stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, spinal cord injury)
social_history: Limited access to a toilet at work or during travel

chief_complaints.text: I have to go to the bathroom all the time
When I have to go, I have to go right now
I get up several times at night to urinate
Sometimes I leak before I can get to the toilet

hpi.onset: Gradual, often over months to years
hpi.duration: Usually present for months to years before the patient seeks care
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive; symptoms may fluctuate with fluid intake, caffeine, and stress
hpi.quality: Sudden, strong urge to urinate that is hard to postpone
hpi.severity: Bothersome and disruptive to daily activities, sleep, and social life; severity varies
hpi.timing: Daytime frequency and nocturia; urgency episodes occur throughout the day

associated_symptoms.text: Urinary frequency (eight or more times a day)
Nocturia (two or more times a night)

argues_against: Primary psychiatric cause of urinary symptoms

atypical.how_it_differs: Symptoms may be attributed to normal aging or coexisting conditions; nocturia and falls may be the main concerns rather than urgency.
Frequency and urgency are common in pregnancy due to uterine pressure and increased fluid volume; symptoms often resolve postpartum.
Polyuria from hyperglycemia can mimic frequency; urgency may be less prominent than large-volume urination.
Increased intra-abdominal pressure can worsen urgency and incontinence; weight loss may improve symptoms.

general.moderate: Comfortable at rest but visibly anxious about access to a toilet; may excuse themselves during the visit
general.severe: Restless or embarrassed, may wear protective padding; otherwise well-appearing
general.critical: Not applicable; overactive bladder is not a critical illness

findings.maneuver: Inspect and palpate the abdomen, including suprapubic percussion for a distended bladder
findings.finding: Soft, non-tender abdomen with no suprapubic fullness or palpable bladder

findings.maneuver: Inspect the external genitalia and, in men, palpate the testes and penis
findings.finding: Normal external genitalia without lesions, discharge, or mass

findings.maneuver: Perform a digital rectal exam in men to assess prostate size, nodularity, and sphincter tone
findings.finding: Smooth, non-nodular prostate; normal anal sphincter tone

findings.maneuver: Perform a pelvic exam in women to inspect for atrophy, prolapse, or mass and to assess for pelvic floor weakness
findings.finding: Normal vaginal mucosa without atrophy or mass; no significant prolapse; no pelvic floor tenderness

findings.maneuver: Test lower extremity strength, sensation, deep tendon reflexes, and gait; assess perineal sensation and anal wink if neurologic disease is suspected
findings.finding: Normal strength, sensation, reflexes, and gait; intact perineal sensation and anal wink
Alert and oriented with normal cognition
No suprapubic tenderness or palpable bladder

labs.caveat: Mild sterile pyuria can occur without infection; a positive leukocyte esterase with nitrite or bacteria points to urinary tract infection instead.
A positive nitrite suggests a urinary tract infection rather than overactive bladder and should prompt treatment and reassessment.
Microscopic hematuria in a patient with irritative voiding symptoms warrants evaluation for bladder cancer or stone.
Bacteria in the urine suggest infection, not overactive bladder.
Pyuria is not a feature of uncomplicated overactive bladder; consider infection, stone, or malignancy.
Hyperglycemia causes osmotic polyuria that mimics frequency; screen because diabetes is a common contributor.
Identifies undiagnosed diabetes as a cause of polyuria and frequency.
Elevated creatinine suggests chronic kidney disease or obstruction and should be evaluated before attributing symptoms to overactive bladder.
Negative. Pregnancy causes frequency and urgency and must be excluded in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or treatment.

imaging.preferred_when: When incomplete emptying or retention is suspected

findings.text: Normal bladder wall thickness and no significant post-void residual
Elevated post-void residual suggesting incomplete emptying or outlet obstruction
Bladder wall thickening or trabeculation suggesting chronic obstruction

imaging.preferred_when: Suspected obstruction, stone, or upper tract disease

findings.text: Normal kidneys and bladder without hydronephrosis or stone

imaging.preferred_when: Gross or persistent microscopic hematuria, or suspicion of malignancy or stone

findings.text: No mass, stone, or urothelial thickening
Bladder mass or urothelial thickening suggesting malignancy

imaging.preferred_when: Hematuria, suspected bladder cancer, or refractory symptoms

findings.text: Normal bladder mucosa without tumor or lesion
Bladder tumor or suspicious mucosal lesion

initial.why: Screens for infection, hematuria, glucosuria, and other causes of irritative voiding symptoms
Excludes diabetes as a cause of polyuria and frequency
Assesses incomplete emptying and bladder wall changes
initial.only_if: incomplete emptying, retention, or obstruction is suspected

supporting.why: Confirms or excludes diabetes when glucose is borderline or elevated
Assesses kidney function when obstruction or chronic kidney disease is a concern
Excludes pregnancy as a cause of frequency and urgency
Evaluates for obstruction, stone, or upper tract disease
supporting.only_if: obstruction, stone, or upper tract disease is suspected

not_indicated.why: Not routinely needed unless infection, anemia, or malignancy is suspected
Not routinely needed in uncomplicated overactive bladder
No role in the evaluation of overactive bladder
No role in the evaluation of overactive bladder
Reserved for hematuria or suspected malignancy or stone
not_indicated.only_if: gross or persistent microscopic hematuria, or malignancy or stone is suspected

not_indicated.why: Reserved for hematuria, suspected bladder cancer, or refractory symptoms
not_indicated.only_if: hematuria, suspected bladder cancer, or refractory symptoms are present

decision_points: Exclude urinary tract infection with urinalysis before attributing symptoms to overactive bladder
Check post-void residual when incomplete emptying or retention is suspected
Evaluate hematuria for malignancy or stone rather than assuming overactive bladder
Exclude pregnancy in anyone who could be pregnant before imaging or treatment

criteria.name: Overactive bladder syndrome
criteria.summary: Urgency with or without urge incontinence, usually with daytime frequency and nocturia, in the absence of urinary tract infection or other obvious pathology.
items: Urgency: a sudden, compelling desire to urinate that is difficult to defer
Frequency: usually eight or more voids per day
Nocturia: waking two or more times at night to urinate
Urge incontinence may or may not be present
No infection or other identifiable cause

differential.name: Urinary tract infection
differential.why_considered: Frequency, urgency and nocturia are classic irritative voiding symptoms of cystitis
differential.trigger: Dysuria, cloudy or malodorous urine, or acute onset over days

history: Acute onset over days rather than months
Fever or chills if upper tract involved
imaging: Not routinely needed; renal ultrasound or CT if pyelonephritis with obstruction is suspected

differential.name: Bladder cancer
differential.why_considered: Irritative voiding symptoms including frequency and urgency can be the presenting complaint, especially with carcinoma in situ
differential.trigger: Gross or persistent microscopic hematuria, or refractory irritative symptoms in a smoker

exam: Usually normal; may have a palpable pelvic mass in advanced disease
labs: Urine cytology may show malignant cells
imaging: Bladder mass or urothelial thickening on CT urography
Bladder tumor or suspicious mucosal lesion on cystoscopy

differential.name: Benign prostatic hyperplasia
differential.why_considered: Common in older men and causes frequency, nocturia and urgency from bladder outlet obstruction

exam: Enlarged, smooth, non-nodular prostate on digital rectal exam
labs: Normal urinalysis unless complicated by infection
imaging: Bladder ultrasound showing elevated post-void residual or bladder wall trabeculation

differential.name: Diabetes mellitus
differential.why_considered: Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycemia produces polyuria and frequency that mimic overactive bladder

history: Large-volume urination rather than small voids
labs: Elevated fasting glucose or random glucose

differential.name: Urinary incontinence (stress or mixed)
differential.why_considered: Leakage of urine is a shared symptom and often coexists with overactive bladder

history: Leakage with coughing, sneezing, laughing or lifting rather than with urgency
No strong urge preceding the leak
exam: Leakage demonstrated with Valsalva or cough
Pelvic floor weakness or prolapse on pelvic exam

differential.name: Interstitial cystitis (bladder pain syndrome)
differential.why_considered: Chronic frequency and urgency with pelvic discomfort can be mistaken for overactive bladder

history: Chronic pelvic pain that worsens as the bladder fills and improves with voiding
Symptoms worse with certain foods or during menses
labs: Normal urinalysis and negative urine culture
imaging: Normal bladder on cystoscopy; Hunner lesions may be seen in some patients

differential.name: Neurologic bladder dysfunction
differential.why_considered: Detrusor overactivity from central or peripheral neurologic disease causes urgency and frequency

history: Known stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis or spinal cord injury
exam: Abnormal lower extremity strength, sensation or reflexes
Impaired perineal sensation or absent anal wink
labs: Normal urinalysis unless complicated by infection
imaging: Brain or spinal cord imaging if a new neurologic lesion is suspected
Urodynamics showing detrusor overactivity or dyssynergia

severity.mild: Occasional urgency and frequency that are bothersome but do not limit daily activities or sleep; no or rare urge incontinence
severity.moderate: Daily urgency and frequency with nocturia and occasional urge incontinence; patient plans activities around toilet access and quality of life is affected
severity.severe: Frequent urgency with regular urge incontinence, marked nocturia and sleep disruption; patient avoids social activities, wears protective pads, and is significantly distressed
severity.critical: Not applicable; overactive bladder is not a life-threatening condition

red_flags.meaning: Suggests bladder cancer, stone or other urothelial pathology and requires urologic evaluation
Suggests urinary tract infection or pyelonephritis rather than overactive bladder

red_flags.finding: Sudden severe pelvic or abdominal pain
red_flags.meaning: Suggests stone, torsion or another acute process and needs urgent evaluation

red_flags.finding: New neurologic deficits or saddle anesthesia
red_flags.meaning: Suggests spinal cord or cauda equina pathology and is an emergency

red_flags.finding: Inability to urinate with a palpable bladder
red_flags.meaning: Suggests urinary retention or obstruction and requires immediate catheterization and evaluation
Raises concern for malignancy and warrants further workup

complications.name: Sleep disruption and daytime fatigue
clues: Nocturia two or more times per night

complications.name: Skin irritation or breakdown from incontinence
Falls and fractures
clues: Older adult rushing to the toilet at night

special_populations.differences: Symptoms are often attributed to normal aging; nocturia and falls may be the main concerns rather than urgency. Antimuscarinic side effects such as confusion and constipation are more likely, so beta-3 agonists or behavioral therapy may be preferred.
Frequency and urgency are common in pregnancy from uterine pressure and increased fluid volume and often resolve postpartum; treatment focuses on behavioral measures and pelvic floor exercises.
Polyuria from hyperglycemia can mimic frequency; urgency may be less prominent than large-volume urination. Optimizing glycemic control may improve symptoms.
Increased intra-abdominal pressure worsens urgency and incontinence; weight loss can improve symptoms and should be encouraged.

key_questions.question: Do you get a sudden, strong urge to urinate that you can't put off?
key_questions.looking_for: Urgency, the defining symptom of overactive bladder

key_questions.question: How many times a day do you urinate, and how many times do you get up at night?
key_questions.looking_for: Eight or more voids a day and two or more episodes of nocturia

key_questions.question: Do you ever leak urine before you can reach the toilet?
key_questions.looking_for: Urge incontinence, which may or may not be present

key_questions.question: When did this start, and has it been getting worse?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual onset over months to years rather than an acute illness

key_questions.question: How much do these symptoms bother you or limit your daily activities and sleep?
key_questions.looking_for: Degree of bother and impact on quality of life, which guides treatment

key_questions.question: Does it hurt or burn when you urinate?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; dysuria points to infection or another cause

key_questions.question: Have you seen blood in your urine?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; hematuria requires evaluation for cancer or stone

key_questions.question: Do you have a weak stream, trouble starting, or a feeling that you don't empty your bladder?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; present suggests bladder outlet obstruction such as benign prostatic hyperplasia

key_questions.question: How much fluid, caffeine, and alcohol do you drink each day?
key_questions.looking_for: High intake of fluids, caffeine, or alcohol that worsens urgency and frequency

key_questions.question: What medications do you take, including diuretics?
key_questions.looking_for: Diuretics or other drugs that increase urine output and mimic the symptoms

key_questions.question: Have you had a stroke, Parkinson disease, multiple sclerosis, or a spinal cord injury?
key_questions.looking_for: Neurologic disease that could cause a neurogenic bladder

key_questions.question: Do you have diabetes, or have you had repeated urinary tract infections?
key_questions.looking_for: Conditions that cause polyuria or irritative voiding symptoms

key_questions.question: Any numbness, weakness, trouble walking, or changes in bowel or bladder control?
key_questions.looking_for: Absent; new neurologic deficits suggest a spinal cord or cauda equina process

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, which causes frequency and urgency and must be excluded before treatment

reasoning_points: Urgency is the defining symptom, usually with daytime frequency and nocturia
Urge incontinence may or may not be present
Symptoms are chronic and gradual, not acute over days
Urinalysis is negative for infection, hematuria, and glucosuria
Post-void residual is normal, arguing against obstruction or incomplete emptying
Other causes such as urinary tract infection, bladder cancer, benign prostatic hyperplasia, diabetes, and neurologic disease have been considered and excluded
The diagnosis is clinical, supported by a voiding diary

easy: Older woman with classic urgency, frequency, and nocturia
Symptoms present for months to years
Normal urinalysis and normal post-void residual
No red flags such as hematuria, dysuria, or fever
medium: Older man with coexisting benign prostatic hyperplasia and a weak stream
Patient with diabetes whose polyuria mimics frequency
Woman with mixed urge and stress incontinence
Symptoms worsened by high caffeine or fluid intake
hard: Older adult whose nocturia and falls are the main concern rather than urgency
Patient with microscopic hematuria requiring evaluation for bladder cancer
Patient with Parkinson disease or prior stroke and a neurogenic bladder
Symptoms refractory to initial therapy, raising concern for interstitial cystitis or malignancy
